title: Multi-level Random-Telegraph Noise Mitigation using a Single Spectator Qubit
authors: Yanan Liu, Hongting Song, Areeya Chantasri, Howard M. Wiseman
abstract: Preserving quantum coherence in the presence of environmental noise is one of the principal challenges for quantum technologies. Noise mitigation using spectator qubits (SQs) has recently emerged as a promising approach, enabling indirect probing of the noise without disturbing the data qubit (DQ). However, existing analyses that probe ultimate performance have been restricted to two-state random telegraph process noise, which does not capture more complex noise processes that may arise in the environment. Therefore, we here develop a SQ-based noise mitigation for DQs subject to general multi-level fluctuator noise. We first derive the coherence dynamics of the DQ under such noise, then develop a mitigation scheme in which information about the noise is inferred from sequential SQ measurements and used for phase correction. A memory-efficient heuristic adaptive protocol is proposed to dynamically select the SQ measurement time and angle based on the current noise estimate. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed strategy significantly suppresses decoherence under multi-level noise, achieving performance comparable to that in the two-level case despite the increased complexity of the noise process.
summary: This paper introduces a novel method to protect quantum coherence in a data qubit from general multi-level environmental noise using measurements on a spectator qubit. The core contribution is a memory-efficient, adaptive protocol that dynamically optimizes measurement timing and angles based on the estimated noise state. This demonstrates robust decoherence suppression even when the noise environment is significantly more complex than previously modeled.
main_problem: The primary challenge is preserving quantum coherence of a data qubit (DQ) when subjected to complex, multi-level environmental noise.
main_result: A proposed heuristic adaptive protocol successfully suppresses decoherence under general multi-level noise, achieving performance comparable to simpler two-state noise models.
method: The authors developed a mitigation scheme that infers the unknown noise state from sequential measurements performed on an auxiliary spectator qubit (SQ) and uses this information for phase correction.
model_or_system: The system consists of a DQ and an SQ interacting with an environment causing multi-level random telegraph noise, modeled by $L$ discrete noise levels. The dynamics are governed by time-dependent frequency shifts ($	ilde{\kappa}(t), 	ilde{K}(t)$) derived from the noise state.
key_observables: Coherence ($C_c$), decoherence rate ($\Gamma$), and the probability vector $\vec{A}_n$ tracking the estimated noise state.
important_parameters: The number of noise levels $L$, the transition rates $\gamma_{ij}$, and the measurement parameters (time $	au_n$ and angle $	heta_n$).
main_assumptions: It is assumed that the SQ sensitivities ($K_j$) are non-degenerate relative to the DQ sensitivities ($\kappa_j$), otherwise, the noise distinction fails.
figures_summary: Figure 2 numerically compares decoherence vs. time for 'no-control,' fixed measurements, and the Heuristic Adaptive Algorithm, showing the adaptive method significantly outperforms others and stays below the analytical upper bound.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from deriving coherence dynamics under multi-level noise to developing a measurement-based mitigation scheme using map-based formalism. It then introduces and details a memory-efficient heuristic adaptive protocol for selecting optimal measurement settings ($	au_{n+1}, 	heta_{n+1}$) based on the current noise estimate.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses open quantum systems by providing an advanced, adaptive control strategy to combat realistic, complex environmental noise sources beyond simple two-level approximations.

The or- ange and blue arrows describe the state vectors of the two plausible SQ’s phases: ∣Φ⟩s = ∣Kµτ⟩s and ∣Φ⟩s = ∣Kντ⟩s, cor- responding to the noise levels µ and ν, respectively. The al- gorithm chooses τn+1 based on the time when the two phases are at an angle π apart as in Eq. (44). The black arrow describes the measurement angle θn+1, which is now shown to be at a random angle in the plot, but it should be equal to max{Kµτn+1, Kντn+1}, i.e., either aligned with ∣Kµτ⟩s or ∣Kντ⟩s, following Eq. (45).

FIG. 2. The decoherence as a function of time under different measurement strategies. The black dots correspond to the no-control case. The gray dots represent a fixed measurement angle and time: θ = 1 and τ = π/Mean(K). The magenta dots correspond to the fixed measurement angle and time: θ = π/2 and τ = π/Mean(K). The red, blue, and green curves show the results of the Heuristic Adaptive Algorithm with three initial measurement settings, i.e., case 1, case 2 and case 3. The orange solid line is the upper bound from (52). The inset displays a zoomed-in view.
